Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)
- Summary assessment: Acute viral upper respiratory infection / influenza-like illness with mild dyspnea; feverish sensations; rhinorrhea; sore throat; fatigue; onset ~4–5 days ago. Known risk factors include type 2 diabetes and overweight. No objective vitals or imaging documented.
- Relevant differential diagnoses aligned with transcript:
  - Acute viral upper respiratory infection / influenza-like illness — High
  - Acute bronchitis (viral/post-viral) — Moderate
  - Early community-acquired pneumonia — Moderate
  - ACE inhibitor cough — Low to Moderate
- Conflicts: Conflict noted. (No explicit conflicts between transcript and core DDx; ACEi cough is considered as a potential contributing factor but not the sole explanation.)

Management Plan
- management_plan_main: Supportive care with self-limited course expected. Rest and adequate fluids. If febrile, treat fever with acetaminophen. Antibiotics offered if not improving within 24–48 hours; follow-up if not better by next week.
- Medications prescribed:
  - Amoxicillin: dose/route/frequency: 1 tablet three times daily; route not documented; duration not documented
  - Acetaminophen: dose/route/frequency not documented (as advised for fever/discomfort)
- Follow-up: If symptoms persist or worsen, return in 1 week or sooner if increased shortness of breath or fever persists beyond 24–48 hours.
- Lifestyle/health maintenance: Advise continued hydration and rest; reinforce smoking/vaping reduction; discuss alcohol use with emphasis on overall health.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)
- Acute viral upper respiratory infection / influenza-like illness — High: classic viral prodrome with cough, rhinorrhea, sore throat, fatigue, feverish sensations; onset within days; generally self-limited.
- Acute bronchitis — Moderate: post-viral cough with mild dyspnea; lack of productive sputum.
- Early community-acquired pneumonia — Moderate: dyspnea and feverish symptoms in a patient with diabetes/obesity; absence of focal exam findings or imaging.
- ACE inhibitor cough — Low to Moderate: lisinopril use; dry cough possible but not clearly isolated from broader viral illness.
- Allergic/allergic-like symptoms — Low: rhinorrhea and throat irritation possible; feverish symptoms favor infectious etiologies.
